title: Design a Notification System
summary: Fanning a single event out across push, email, and SMS reliably — without spamming users or ignoring their preferences.

slides.markdown:
Design a system that takes one triggering event — "your order shipped," "someone liked your post" — and reliably fans it out across push, email, and SMS, respecting what each user actually wants to be notified about and how.

Think of it like a mailroom: one memo comes in, and the mailroom decides who gets a copy, which channel to use per recipient (desk drop, email, urgent courier), and makes sure the same memo doesn't get delivered twice to the same person. The hard part isn't sending one notification — it's doing that reliably at the scale of one event reaching millions of people without becoming spam.

**Functional:** trigger a notification for a user across one or more channels (push, email, SMS), respecting per-user, per-channel preferences (opted out of marketing email, wants push only for security alerts, and so on).

**Non-functional:** each channel has its own delivery SLA — push should land in seconds, email tolerates minutes, SMS is costly enough to reserve for high-priority events. The system must survive **at-least-once** upstream event delivery without turning that into duplicate notifications reaching the user.

**Explicit non-goal:** this is delivery infrastructure, not the marketing team's campaign-authoring UI — building templates and scheduling broadcast campaigns is a separate, higher-level product.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: events, targets, and peak notification volume
slides.markdown:
Take 10,000 triggering events/sec platform-wide on an ordinary day. Most target one user (a like, a shipping update) but a broadcast event — a platform-wide announcement, a service outage notice — can target all 200M users in a single trigger.

One such broadcast, fanned out across even just push and email, produces 400M individual sends from a single event — at 50,000 sends/sec sustained, that's over two hours just to drain one event, during which ordinary per-user events are still arriving and need to interleave fairly, not queue behind the broadcast.

The sizing lesson: provision for the fan-out multiplier of your *worst* single event, not the average one.

`sendNotification(userId, template, channelHints)` is the trigger call — `channelHints` suggests urgency (e.g. "security") without forcing a specific channel, since the actual channel is resolved against the user's preferences downstream. A separate `updatePreferences(userId, channel, category, enabled)` API lets users opt in or out per channel and per notification category (marketing vs security vs social).

Keeping preference updates as their own API, decoupled from the send path, matters: it means every future trigger reads current preferences at send time rather than baking a stale opt-in decision into the event itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Data model: templates, preferences, and a delivery log
slides.markdown:
Three tables carry the system. **Templates** hold the message shape per notification type, parameterized ("Your order #{orderId} shipped"), so a code change isn't needed to tweak copy. **Preferences** map `(userId, category, channel) -> enabled`, checked before every send. **Delivery log** records `(eventId, userId, channel)` for every attempted send, keyed so a retry of the same event can check "did I already send this?" before sending again.

The delivery log is the piece easiest to skip and most important not to — it's what turns at-least-once event delivery into effectively-once notifications reaching the user.

![Notification pipeline flowing from a triggering event through template lookup to per-recipient channel dispatch, branching into push, email, and SMS adapters](assets/notification-pipeline.svg)

Each stage in this pipeline maps to a real decision: template lookup exists so copy isn't hardcoded per event type; the branch into per-channel adapters exists because push, email, and SMS each speak to a completely different external provider with its own API and failure modes.

assets.alt: Notification pipeline flowing from a triggering event through template lookup to per-recipient channel dispatch, branching into push, email, and SMS adapters

slides.markdown:
A single broadcast event doesn't expand into millions of sends synchronously — it's enqueued once, and a worker pool pulls user IDs from the target audience in batches, resolving preferences and dispatching per user, per channel, independently.

This is the same shape as fan-out-on-write in a news feed: one write (the event), many downstream deliveries, done asynchronously so the triggering call returns immediately rather than blocking until all 200M sends complete.

Because upstream events can be delivered more than once (a queue redelivering after a slow ack, a producer retrying after a timeout), the dispatch worker checks the delivery log for `(eventId, userId, channel)` before sending — if it's already there, skip, don't resend.

Throttling is a separate concern layered on top: even for a legitimately new event, cap how many notifications a single user receives in a short window (say, no more than 5 push notifications in 10 minutes for non-critical categories), queuing or dropping the excess rather than burying the user in a burst.

Before any send, the dispatch worker checks the user's preference for that `(category, channel)` pair — if disabled, the send is skipped and logged as suppressed, not silently dropped, so support and analytics can see it was a deliberate opt-out.

**Quiet hours** add a time dimension: a user in a category that allows push might still have marked 11pm-7am local time as do-not-disturb. Non-critical notifications queue until quiet hours end; critical ones (a security alert, a fraud warning) bypass quiet hours entirely by design, since the cost of a late security alert outweighs the cost of one interrupted night.

A failed push send (app uninstalled, device token expired) doesn't mean the notification is lost — for high-priority categories, the dispatch worker falls back to the next channel in the user's configured order, typically email. Low-priority categories may simply drop a failed send rather than escalate.

Each fallback attempt is still logged in the delivery log under its own `(eventId, userId, channel)` key, so falling back to email after a failed push is treated as its own deliverable, deduplicated independently — not a retry of the same channel.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: synchronous send vs queued/async send
slides.markdown:
| | Synchronous send | Queued/async send |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger call latency | Blocks until the provider responds | Returns immediately after enqueueing |
| Failure handling | Caller must handle provider errors inline | Retries and fallback handled by the worker, invisibly to the caller |
| Scales to broadcast events | No — one caller thread can't send to 200M users | Yes — worker pool drains the queue independently |
| Best for | A single, latency-critical, one-off send | Everything else, especially anything that can fan out |

**How to decide:** default to async for anything that fans out to more than a handful of recipients — the trigger path should never be coupled to how long the slowest external provider takes to respond.

![End-to-end architecture from event source through the ingestion queue, worker pool, delivery log, and per-channel adapters](assets/end-to-end-architecture.svg)

The delivery log appears twice in this picture — read before sending (dedup) and written after (so the next redelivery of the same event sees it) — which is what makes the whole pipeline idempotent under at-least-once event delivery.

assets.alt: End-to-end architecture from event source through the ingestion queue, worker pool, delivery log, and per-channel adapters

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: a channel provider rate-limiting the whole system
slides.markdown:
APNs, FCM, and SMS gateways all enforce their own rate limits, independent of how fast your own workers can produce sends. If the worker pool dispatches to a single provider faster than that provider accepts, you get throttling errors — and if the worker pool retries those immediately, it can make the rate limiting worse, not better.

The fix is per-provider rate limiting *on your side*, matched to the provider's documented ceiling, with backoff on 429/throttle responses. Crucially, one provider's rate limit shouldn't stall the other channels' queues — each channel needs its own independent queue and worker capacity so a slow SMS gateway doesn't delay push notifications.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a retry storm re-sending the same notification to every user
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If a broadcast send partially fails, just retry the whole event from the top."

**Why it's wrong:** re-running the full fan-out re-sends to every user who already received it successfully, not just the ones who failed — for a 200M-user broadcast, that's potentially 200M duplicate notifications from one retry.

**Correct model:** retry at the level of individual failed `(eventId, userId, channel)` entries, using the delivery log to identify exactly which sends didn't succeed, and resume only those — never re-trigger the whole event.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: no dedup key, double-enqueue under at-least-once delivery
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our event queue rarely redelivers, so we don't need a dedup check before sending."

**Why it's wrong:** at-least-once delivery isn't a rare edge case, it's the documented contract of most event queues — redelivery *will* happen under normal operation (consumer crash before ack, network blip), and without a dedup key, every redelivery becomes a fresh, duplicate notification the user actually sees.

**Correct model:** every event needs a stable `eventId` carried through to the delivery log, checked before every send, no matter how rare redelivery seems in testing — the whole point of the log is to make dispatch idempotent under a delivery guarantee that explicitly allows duplicates.

slides.sectionTitle: Summary: template + preference + queue + adapter, dedup as the safety net
slides.markdown:
The whole system is a queue absorbing bursty, fan-out-shaped events; a worker pool that checks preferences and quiet hours before dispatching; per-channel provider adapters with their own rate limits and retry/fallback logic; and a delivery log tying every attempt back to a stable event ID so retries never become user-visible duplicates.

The same at-least-once, dedup-on-receipt philosophy reappears in a system's presence updates and in chat's own delivery guarantees — this pipeline is really the general-purpose version of "deliver this reliably, once, to whoever should get it."
